name: THE YOU CAN LEAD A HORSERADISH TO WATERCRESS BURGER

recipe.history:
Horseradish — Armoracia rusticana — is a perennial plant of the Brassicaceae family, native to southeastern Europe and western Asia, and one of the most ancient condiment plants known to human cultivation. Its fiery, sinus-clearing heat comes not from capsaicin, as in chili peppers, but from allyl isothiocyanate, the same volatile compound responsible for the heat of wasabi and mustard — a compound released only when the root is grated or damaged, as enzymes and glucosinolates combine in the presence of water. The ancient Egyptians knew the horseradish root and it appears in records dating to 1500 BCE; the ancient Greeks used it as a rub for lower back pain and as an aphrodisiac, which suggests the ancient Greeks were having a more interesting time than their writings usually suggest. It is one of the five bitter herbs of the Jewish Passover Seder — maror — and has been central to Central and Eastern European cooking for centuries, where it appears as a sauce, a condiment, and a preservative. The classic Austrian Tafelspitz would be unthinkable without its braised beef-and-horseradish pairing, a marriage that speaks across millennia to the specific chemical affinity between the glucosinolate heat of the root and the fatty, mineral depth of beef.

Horseradish arrived in North America with European settlers in the 1600s and spread widely because the plant grows aggressively and is nearly impossible to eradicate once established in suitable soil — a metaphor, perhaps, for how forcefully it embeds itself in every cooking tradition it touches. American horseradish culture developed most strongly in the Midwest, particularly in Illinois, which still produces the majority of the world's commercial horseradish supply in the rich soils around Collinsville. The bottled prepared horseradish — grated root preserved in white vinegar — became a fixture of the American table alongside roast beef, on corned beef sandwiches, in cocktail sauce for shrimp, and mixed into Bloody Marys. Its application to burgers is a natural extension of its centuries-old relationship with beef, and paired with watercress — the sharp, peppery aquatic green that has been eaten in Europe since the time of the ancient Greeks — it creates one of the most intellectually coherent burger toppings imaginable: heat on top of heat, peppery on top of peppery, each amplifying and defining the other.

I first encountered freshly grated horseradish — as opposed to the prepared bottled kind — at a Jewish delicatessen that made it in-house, pulled from roots in a bucket, grated on a box grater in the back with what the counter man described as 'appropriate suffering.' He handed me a small paper cup of it and the fumes hit my eyes before the taste hit my tongue. For about ten seconds I couldn't see clearly and my sinuses felt like they had been reintroduced to the concept of air. Then the heat faded and left behind this bright, clean, almost sweet sharpness that made every other flavor on my corned beef sandwich snap into focus. That is what fresh horseradish does — it is a lens that sharpens everything around it. I grate it fresh for this burger.

The medium-rare burger — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — and horseradish have a specific relationship that goes beyond mere compatibility. The gentle residual warmth of a properly rested medium-rare patty is exactly sufficient to bloom the volatile compounds in the fresh horseradish cream spread on the bun, releasing additional heat and pungency without cooking them away entirely. The pink juices of the patty flow into the watercress and the horseradish cream, softening the heat of the former and enriching the bitterness of the latter. Cook that patty to well done and you lose the juice, lose the bloom, lose the aliveness — and what you have is a dry beef disc under a fine sauce that deserves better company. Medium rare is the only temperature that treats this burger as the serious thing it is.
ingredients: 1 egg white beaten with 1 tablespoon water (for egg wash)
3 tablespoons freshly grated horseradish root (or 2 tablespoons prepared horseradish, well drained)
2 large bunches fresh watercress, thick stems removed
Pinch of freshly cracked black pepper
6 slices sharp white cheddar or aged Gruyère (about 1 oz each)
1/2 small red onion, very thinly sliced, soaked in cold water 10 minutes and drained
Extra virgin olive oil for finishing
instructions: 1. MAKE THE KAISER ROLLS: Combine warm water, warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 to 8 minutes until foamy.
2. Add flour, salt, butter, and egg. Mix on low with the dough hook 2 minutes until combined. Increase to medium and knead 10 to 12 minutes until a smooth, slightly tacky dough forms.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise at room temperature 1 to 1 1/2 hours until doubled.

4. Punch down and divide into 6 equal portions. Shape each into a round ball. For the traditional kaiser stamp, use a kaiser roll stamp if you have one. Alternatively, use scissors to snip 5 cuts radiating from the center of each roll to create the signature pinwheel pattern.
5. Place on parchment-lined baking sheets. Cover and proof 45 minutes to 1 hour until puffed.
6. Preheat oven to 425°F (220°C). Brush rolls with egg white wash. Sprinkle generously with poppy seeds. Bake 14 to 16 minutes until golden brown and hollow-sounding when tapped. Cool on a wire rack.

7. MAKE THE HORSERADISH CREAM: If using fresh horseradish root, peel and grate finely — do this in a well-ventilated area as the fumes are genuinely powerful. Combine grated or prepared horseradish, crème fraîche, sour cream, whole-grain mustard, lemon juice, sugar, salt, and chives in a small bowl. Stir well. Taste and adjust horseradish and lemon. Cover and refrigerate at least 30 minutes for the flavors to meld.
8. PREPARE THE WATERCRESS: Just before assembly, toss watercress with olive oil, lemon juice, a pinch of flaky salt, and black pepper. The watercress should be lightly dressed, not saturated.

9. FORM THE PATTIES: Gently combine ground chuck and ground sirloin in a large bowl. Season with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Form into 6 patties, 4 1/2 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, with a shallow center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.
10. COOK THE PATTIES: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties without pressing, 3 minutes on the first side until a deep brown crust forms.

11. Flip once. Lay a slice of sharp white cheddar or Gruyère over each patty. Cook 2 to 2 1/2 minutes more. Check internal temperature — target 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Transfer to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.
12. TOAST THE ROLLS: Split kaiser rolls and toast cut-side down in a hot dry skillet 60 to 90 seconds.
13. ASSEMBLE: Spread horseradish cream generously on both cut sides of each kaiser roll — be liberal here, the horseradish cream is the soul of this burger.
14. Place a handful of dressed watercress on the bottom bun. Add tomato slices. Add the rested, cheese-topped patty.
15. Top with drained red onion slices. Drizzle lightly with extra virgin olive oil and finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
